name: NAD+

b.x: A 398% spike in plasma levels after one six-hour drip. That single data point from a 2019 pilot study [1] turned NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide, CAS 53-84-9) from a biochemistry footnote into one of the most discussed molecules in longevity circles. NAD+ sits at the center of cellular energy metabolism. It shuttles electrons through glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation to produce ATP. It also feeds three enzyme families that control aging: sirtuins (SIRT1 through SIRT7), PARPs for DNA repair, and CD38, an ectoenzyme whose activity rises with age and is now considered a primary driver of NAD+ decline. Between ages 40 and 60, cellular NAD+ drops roughly 50%. The practical question is whether restoring those levels from the outside actually changes outcomes. For addiction recovery, the answer looks promising. The BR+NAD protocol (500 to 1,500 mg/day IV over 10 days) reduced craving scores from 5.9 to 0.22 in 50 substance use disorder patients [2]. For general wellness and anti-aging, the community runs ahead of the science. Hundreds of threads across r/Nootropics, r/longevity, and r/Peptides consistently report improved energy, reduced brain fog, and better exercise recovery with subcutaneous dosing at 100 to 250 mg twice weekly. A 2024 systematic review [3] confirmed safety across clinical conditions but called the efficacy evidence "heterogeneous." Science has not refuted the wellness case; data simply lags community adoption.

NAD+ is a central metabolic coenzyme in oxidized (NAD+) and reduced (NADH) forms. It passes electrons through three energy-generating pathways: glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and the electron transport chain. Without adequate NAD+, ATP production slows at every step. Beyond energy, NAD+ is the required substrate for sirtuins (SIRT1 through SIRT7), a family of deacetylases that regulate gene expression, mitochondrial biogenesis, and inflammatory signaling. SIRT1 and SIRT3 are the two most studied in longevity research. When NAD+ levels rise, SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of PGC-1alpha increases, promoting new mitochondrial formation and improved oxidative capacity. PARPs (poly-ADP-ribose polymerases) consume NAD+ to repair DNA breaks. After genotoxic stress, PARP1 activation can drain the cellular NAD+ pool rapidly; this is one reason PARP inhibitor cancer drugs work by keeping NAD+ low. Exogenous NAD+ supplementation directly opposes that mechanism. CD38, an ectoenzyme that degrades NAD+, rises with age and is now recognized as a primary cause of age-related NAD+ decline. Direct IV or subcutaneous NAD+ administration bypasses the multi-step enzymatic conversion that oral precursors like NMN and NR require. It also supports the NAD+/NADH ratio in the electron transport chain, reducing electron leak and reactive oxygen species production.
NAD+ benefits center on cellular energy restoration, sirtuin activation, and DNA repair support.

Your 500 mg vial with 5 mL bacteriostatic water gives you 100 mg/mL. At 100 mg per dose, that's 1.0 mL (100 units on a U-100 insulin syringe), so one vial covers 5 doses. If you're running 250 mg doses, reconstitute with 2 mL instead: that gives 250 mg/mL, and each dose is 1.0 mL. Trying to pull 2.5 mL for a 250 mg dose from a standard 5 mL reconstitution is impractical for a single subcutaneous site. Inject slowly. Thirty to sixty seconds minimum. The sting is the number one complaint in every forum thread, and speed is almost always the cause. Warm the syringe in your palm for a minute before injecting. Morning dosing is the standard; some users report sleep disruption with evening administration. One thing most beginners miss: cloudiness or any visible precipitate means discard the vial. NAD+ degrades with heat and agitation. Add the water slowly down the vial wall and swirl gently. Never shake it.
Cycling Protocol
Some protocols run continuously at maintenance doses. Higher-dose IV protocols are typically done in short bursts (3-5 days). Subcutaneous dosing can be sustained longer with periodic breaks.

NAD+ functions as a substrate and signaling molecule, not a receptor agonist: receptor desensitization is not the primary concern. The 8-on/2-off structure matches its listed cycle and community consensus. Continuous low-dose maintenance (100 mg 1×/week) is used by some without cycling breaks but lacks safety evidence for this approach.

The most serious safety concern with injectable NAD+ is endotoxin contamination. A compounding pharmacy issued a Class I recall in October 2025 covering its 100 mg/mL and 200 mg/mL NAD+ vials for raised endotoxins; a Class II recall for sterility assurance concerns preceded it in July 2025. Fever or rigors within one to two hours of injection are sentinel signs of endotoxin exposure. Stop immediately, do not reuse the vial, and seek medical evaluation. IV infusion side effects are rate-dependent. Nausea, flushing, chest tightness, and headache occur during the drip and are directly proportional to the infusion speed. Slowing the rate resolves symptoms within minutes in most cases. These are not allergic reactions and do not indicate a defective product. During the BR+NAD addiction protocol (500 to 1,500 mg/day over 5 to 10 hours), these effects are expected and managed by the supervising clinician. Subcutaneous injection stinging is the most common complaint at the home-use level. Injecting slowly over 30 to 60 seconds, warming the solution to room temperature, and using a 27 to 31 gauge insulin syringe all reduce the discomfort. Some injection sites are worse than others; rotating between abdomen and upper thigh helps. Published side effect data beyond the above is limited. The 2024 systematic review [3] confirmed safety across clinical conditions but noted the total number of rigorously studied humans remains small. Most wellness and anti-aging trials have fewer than 50 participants, and many lack placebo controls. Theoretical concerns exist around sustained supraphysiologic PARP and CD38 activation at high chronic doses. No hepatotoxicity has appeared in trials, but safety data for long-term subcutaneous use does not exist. Liver enzymes (ALT and AST) should be checked at baseline and at 8 weeks for anyone dosing at 250 mg or above per session. NAD+ may support rapidly dividing cells. No data exists on its effects in active cancer or a history of malignancy. It should not be combined with PARP inhibitor drugs (olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib), as exogenous NAD+ directly counteracts their mechanism of action. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications since no safety data exists for injectable NAD+ in those populations.
Common Issues & Solutions
Severe injection site sting: Inject over 30–60 seconds (not faster); warm the solution to room temperature before injection; use a 27–31g insulin syringe; try a different abdominal injection site.
Nausea/flushing during IV: Rate-dependent: slow the infusion immediately; symptoms should resolve within minutes of reducing the drip rate; this is not a dangerous reaction or product quality issue.

No perceived effect at 100 mg SubQ: IV plasma half-life is only ~30–45 min; SubQ provides a slower, sustained delivery: subjective effects are subtler than IV; allow 4–6 weeks before judging; check reconstitution integrity (swirl gently, never shake; cloudiness means discard).

Fever or rigors after injection: Stop immediately and do not use the same vial again: this pattern is consistent with endotoxin contamination (see the 2025 Class I recall); contact the pharmacy; seek medical evaluation.
Reconstitution cloudiness or precipitate: NAD+ is heat- and agitation-sensitive; add BAC water slowly down the vial wall and swirl gently; cloudiness indicates degradation: discard.

NAD+ is not FDA-approved as a therapeutic drug. It is available through compounding pharmacies (both 503A and 503B facilities) as a research compound. The FDA has not approved any NAD+ injectable product for anti-aging, wellness, or addiction treatment indications as of October 2026. Compounded NAD+ carries documented quality risk. A 2025 Class I recall for raised endotoxins in compounded NAD+ vials is a concrete example. FDA-registered 503B outsourcing facilities are the more tightly regulated compounding tier. A current Certificate of Analysis showing endotoxin and sterility testing is the minimum safety standard for any batch. NAD+ is not on the WADA prohibited list as of 2026 and is not a controlled substance. Wellness and detox clinics offer IV NAD+ protocols for addiction treatment, but no FDA-approved product carries that indication. FDA lists NAD in 503A Category 1, bulk drug substances under evaluation (May 14, 2026). Beta-NAD sits in 503B Category 1 (March 21, 2025). This content is for research and educational purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice. Consult a licensed healthcare provider before using any injectable compound.

faqs.q: Is subcutaneous NAD+ actually effective, or just a watered-down version of IV?
faqs.a: SubQ bioavailability is near 100% since it bypasses the GI tract entirely. The slower absorption through fat tissue actually reduces the nausea and flushing you get with IV drips. IV produces faster, higher peak levels useful for acute protocols like addiction treatment. For ongoing maintenance, SubQ is practical and effective.

faqs.q: Does the 10-day IV NAD+ protocol really work for addiction cravings?
faqs.a: The BR+NAD protocol delivers 500-1,500 mg/day IV over 5-10 hours for 10 consecutive days with amino acids and B-vitamins. A 2022 study (PMID 36118157) with 50 substance use patients showed craving scores dropping from 5.9 to 0.22 out of 10: that's dramatic. This is the best-supported acute clinical use of IV NAD+.

faqs.q: Why do I feel awful during my NAD+ IV drip?
faqs.a: Nausea, flushing, and chest tightness are rate-dependent side effects from supraphysiologic extracellular NAD+. They're directly proportional to how fast the drip runs. Slow the infusion rate and symptoms typically resolve within minutes. It doesn't mean the product is bad or that you're having a dangerous reaction.

faqs.q: NAD+ IV vs oral NMN/NR: am I wasting money on injections?
faqs.a: For acute loading, IV NAD+ wins: one study showed 398% above baseline (PMID 31572171). But for chronic maintenance, oral NMN or NR may achieve similar steady-state levels at a fraction of the cost. A 2026 head-to-head study (PMID 41704678) showed similar tolerability between IV NAD+ and IV NR. The honest answer is the debate isn't settled yet.

faqs.q: How do I properly reconstitute and store NAD+ for home injection?
faqs.a: Use bacteriostatic water (not sterile water), inject it slowly down the vial wall, and swirl gently: never shake. Use a 27-31g insulin syringe, inject SubQ into abdomen or upper thigh over 30-60 seconds to minimize the sting. Refrigerate at 2-8 degrees C and toss it after 28-30 days. Never freeze reconstituted solution.

faqs.q: What is the recommended NAD+ dosage?
faqs.a: NAD+ dosing varies by experience level. Beginners typically start at 100 mg 2x/week, moderate users at 250 mg 2x/week, and aggressive protocols use 500 mg 3x/week.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of NAD+?
faqs.a: The half-life of NAD+ is Not measured (infused NAD+ is cleared from plasma rapidly; functional effects reported for 2-4 hours). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.
